Former attorney here. (I don't practice anymore. Don't ask me for legal advice unless you're prepared to hand over $75,000 in Bitcoin.)

Coercion is tricky. The law in N.Y. (which is the one my man Julian Assange referenced in his tweet; for what purpose I'm not sure, because I thought CNN was based in Atlanta) says:

§ 135.60 Coercion in the second degree.

A person is guilty of coercion in the second degree when he or she compels or induces a person to engage in conduct which the latter has a legal right to abstain from engaging in, or to abstain from engaging in conduct in which he or she has a legal right to engage, [...]

... which is what happened; the creator of the WWE meme has the right to do so, and he also has the right to publish an infographic about the religious affiliations of the management at CNN.

by means of instilling in him or her a fear that, if the demand is not complied with, the actor or another will:

Here's the crime. In order for something to be a crime, there must be an actus reus (meaning "guilty act") committed with the correct mens rea (meaning "guilty mind"). In other words, you have to perform a certain act while in a certain state of mind. Here, the actus reus is the instilling of fear in the other person, and the mens rea is one of intentionality. Therefore, if you intentionally instill fear in another person that you'll do one of the things on the big laundry-list in § 135.60 unless they comply with your demand, then you're guilty of coercion.

Most of the big laundry-list doesn't apply, but the last one does:

\9. Perform any other act which would not in itself materially benefit the actor but which is calculated to harm another person materially with respect to his or her health, safety, business, calling, career, financial condition, reputation or personal relationships.

In other words, if you say "I will publicly condemn you as a Nazi, release your name and home address and call down screeching SJW harpies upon you", that counts.

The problem here is actually a couple sections further along in the Penal Law:

§ 135.75 Coercion; defense.

In any prosecution for coercion committed by instilling in the victim a fear that he or another person would be charged with a crime,

... such as a "hate crime", for example ...

it is an affirmative defense that the defendant reasonably believed the threatened charge to be true and that his sole purpose was to compel or induce the victim to take reasonable action to make good the wrong which was the subject of such threatened charge.

I think this is arguable. I don't agree with the interpretation, but if CNN was under the mistaken impression that "hate crimes" were a thing (they aren't), that publishing an infographic concerning the religious affiliations of its management constituted a "hate crime" (it doesn't), and it made a threat of "you will be charged with a hate crime" with the sole motivation of getting the meme-creator to apologize for the supposed "hate crime", then they could theoretically weasel their way out of it.

However, if they only said "we will dox you and unleash SJW harpies on your Nazi ass", that defense doesn't apply.

Of course, all of this presupposes that an unreasonable prosecutor would actually press charges in the first place, and good luck getting that to happen.
